overview.text: The strong interaction (strong force) is a fundamental interaction of the Standard Model, described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD). At the smallest scales, it acts on quarks and gluons: gluons carry the interaction, and it binds quarks into protons, neutrons, and other hadrons. Its distinctive color charge is a physics label, not visible color; quarks and gluons are confined inside composite particles rather than found alone in ordinary matter. A residual effect of this interaction also binds protons and neutrons into atomic nuclei, counteracting the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons. Unlike a simple long-range pull, its behavior varies with distance, becoming weaker at very short quark separations.

key_facts.text: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the theory that describes the strong interaction.
Gluons carry the strong interaction, which binds quarks into protons, neutrons, and other composite particles.
A residual effect of the interaction binds protons and neutrons in nuclei, helping overcome the electrical repulsion between protons.
“Color” names a type of charge in this theory; it does not mean that quarks or gluons have visible colors.
The interaction’s strength depends on distance: it is weaker at very short quark separations and stronger as quarks are pulled farther apart.
